rows.evidence: Q1: Methods and Results sections report the authors' own Landsat TM/ETM+ classification for 1995-2010 (overall accuracy 95.1%, Kappa 0.8977), biyearly field surveys 2005-2013 in 125 villages, and analysis of runoff (1962-2011), groundwater table and TDS (1998-2011, 59 and 74 wells) with Mann-Kendall tests (Table 5, Figs. 4-6).
rows.notes: The study uses remote sensing itself as a research tool to map land-use change; it does not report that conservation policies used RS data to set quotas or reduce irrigated area, nor does it link RS to any groundwater recovery. The reported groundwater-table rise (45 cm in the northern oasis 2005-2011, Discussion) and reduced extraction are attributed to the Ecological Construction policy measures: closing 3,161 wells, a watershed water-allocation plan (22% of mountain runoff), and replacing flood with drip/tube irrigation. RS here is a monitoring/mapping precondition, not the technology delivering the effect, and the effect stems from other interventions. Groundwater figures are given as oasis-wide trends with standard-error bars (Fig. 5), but not for an RS-attributable effect.

rows.evidence: Q1: Methods/Results report the authors' own Landsat-based land-use classification (Tables 1-4, Figs. 2-3), field surveys and hydrological/climatic time-series analysis.
rows.notes: The study's own RS result is an increase in shrub land area (Table 1: 116.71 to 160.10 km2, 2005-2010) attributed to afforestation campaigns on degraded farmland and sand land, not to remote sensing. Vegetation cover area is not biodiversity; the only biodiversity-type information (vegetation varieties falling from 19 to 9, community shifts) is cited from other work. The study does not report that RS data was used by policy to deliver ecological recovery; RS is the authors' mapping tool, i.e. upstream of the claimed effect.

rows.evidence: Q1: Methods/Results report own RS classification, field surveys (125 villages, 2005-2013) and runoff/groundwater time-series analysis (Figs. 4-6, Table 5).
rows.notes: Water-conservation outcomes reported in the Discussion (inflow to the oasis rising from 0.97e8 m3 in 2005 to 2.59e8 m3 in 2011; groundwater extraction down 2.4e8 m3; irrigation efficiency from 0.56 to 0.61; consumption down 1500-1800 m3/ha; irrigated area reduced to 41,700 ha) are attributed to the EC policy package: well closure, watershed allocation quotas, drip/tube irrigation on half the irrigated area, and crop restructuring. The study never states that RS data underpinned these quotas or reductions; RS is used only by the authors to map land-use change. Thus the water savings are evidence about drip/tube irrigation and administrative water allocation, not remote sensing. Several of the outcome figures are sourced from the county Water Resource Bureau rather than measured by the authors, and the study notes farmer resistance to drip irrigation and well closure, which is a limitation of the policy, not of an RS result.

notes: Full text appears complete (abstract through references). The paper is a primary mixed-method study (Landsat land-use mapping validated by field survey, hydrological and climate time series, household interviews) on policy-driven land-use and water-resource change in Minqin Oasis. Remote sensing is the authors' analytical instrument for mapping land use; nowhere does the paper report that RS data was used by policy makers to set quotas, reduce irrigated area or monitor recovery, so none of the three claims about RS delivering groundwater recovery, biodiversity or water conservation is supported by the study's own results. The cited review appears to have conflated the study's method with the policy instruments it describes.
